title: The keepers of the record
lede: How a family's memory survived a burnt archive, a destroyed diary and ninety years of retelling.
body: This archive begins with a conversation between a grandfather "coming up to 90" {q:50} and a grandchild with printouts from an online family tree. But the narrator is himself the heir of a long line of family historians, and he begins with them.

"Our interest in genealogy really began with my grandfather", {p:bellingham-arthur-somerville|Bellingham Arthur Somerville} (1856–1916) {q:2}. An RIC officer with a collector's temperament, he followed up every Somerville he saw in a newspaper and wrote notes on what he found, filling "about six volumes" {q:6-8}. Crucially, "he was alive before the fire in the Four Courts, and therefore he had access to records which are no longer available" {q:4}.

{ctx}On 30 June 1922, in the opening battle of the Civil War, an explosion and fire destroyed the Public Record Office of Ireland in the Four Courts, with seven centuries of records including almost all 19th-century census returns and huge numbers of wills and parish registers {s:irishtimes-pro}. For Irish families, notes copied before 1922 are often the only surviving trace of documents that no longer exist {s:tcd-beyond2022}.

His eldest daughter, {p:cecilia-somerville|Cecilia}, "took up her father's interest in genealogy … she was a very good genealogist", active in the learned societies of Dublin {q:230-232}. The family also kept older material: an entry in {t:crisps-visitation|"Crisp's"} with the facsimile signatures of {p:captain-william-somerville|Captain William Somerville} and {p:eliza-bellingham|Eliza Bellingham} {q:124}; transcripts of Captain William's diary {q:132}; letters of Eliza and of her daughter {p:eliza-nelson|Eliza Nelson} in America {q:52, 166}; portraits and a miniature {q:26-28, 36, 44}.

Not everything survived. The diary has "lots of blank spaces because parts of the diary were destroyed": {p:eddie|Aunt Eddie} remembered, as a child, destroying papers after the deaths of the older generation in the 1890s {q:132-134}. "Which is a great shame."

{int}This archive treats the recording as testimony: what a well-informed family historian remembered, often from documents he had read decades before. Where his memory can be checked against published records, it proves remarkably accurate: the three Bellingham sisters and two brothers, Henry's death at Badajoz, the dormancy of the baronetcy in January 1929, the Youghal inquiry, Bunt at Archangel. Where it cannot, we say so.

title: Baronets and Ardrass
lede: A Lord Mayor's baronetcy, a second son's Kildare estate, and the military habit.
body: The narrator traces the line to "the first baronet" {q:84}. {ctx}Sir James Somerville (c. 1698–1748), MP for Dublin City and Lord Mayor of Dublin in 1736–37, was created a baronet "of Somerville, County Meath" in February 1748, months before his death {s:wp-sir-james-somerville}. His eldest son Quaile succeeded him, and the title then passed from father to son through the senior line {s:wp-athlumney}.

The family descend instead from his second son. "Major William Somerville was the second son of the first baronet, and inherited an estate in County Kildare called Ardrass … There was a large house and a lot of land" {q:84-86}. As was usual, "the lands were generally tenanted, leading to the agrarian problems in this country" {q:86}. {ctx}Published sources confirm a second son, Major William, buried at St Audoen's, Dublin {s:wp-sir-james-somerville}, and the National Library holds a registered pedigree of "the Somervilles of Ardrass, Celbridge" beginning in 1752 {s:nli-ardrass}.

{pl:ardrass|Ardrass} did not stay with this branch. Captain William had an interest in the lands, half of which went into his marriage settlement, but "there's no record of him having [lived there]" {q:88-90}. The house survived the political upheavals of the early 20th century only to be pulled down in the 1950s after a great sale of its contents, "the fate of country houses in this country" {q:94-96}.

The senior line went on to public distinction. {ctx}Sir William Meredyth Somerville, 5th Baronet (1802–1873), sat for Drogheda, was Chief Secretary for Ireland through the Famine years 1847–52, and became Baron Athlumney {s:wp-1st-baron}. His son, the 2nd Baron, died childless on 8 January 1929; the peerages became extinct and the baronetcy dormant {s:wp-2nd-baron}. The narrator: "it has been dormant ever since" {q:174}.

"I don't think I ever realised how much of a military family we were", says the interviewer; the narrator lists Major William, Captain William and Bellingham Arthur, mostly in "the county regiments … the equivalent of the territorials" {q:470}.

title: The Bellinghams of Castle Bellingham
lede: Three sisters, two brothers, a French-Canadian bride, a death at Badajoz, and an estate lost to an uncle.
body: "A Captain William Somerville and a lady called Eliza Bellingham, and that is [how] the name came in" {q:20}. The Bellingham name has been carried by Somerville sons ever since, and the narrator's own grandfather was christened Bellingham Arthur {q:24-26}.

"Eliza Bellingham was one of three sisters … They had two brothers", brought up at {pl:castle-bellingham|Castle Bellingham} in Co. Louth {q:26-28}. {ctx}The published genealogy names them exactly: the children of Lt-Col. Henry Bellingham, a Louth Militia officer, and Elizabeth Tenison were Alan (c. 1773–1821), Elizabeth (1779–1839), Dorothea (c. 1780–1848), Henrietta Sophia (b. c. 1782) and Henry Tenison (1784–1812) {s:lf-bellingham}.

The elder brother, {p:alan-bellingham-1773|Alan}, was in the narrator's word "unsuccessful". As a young man he had been in Canada {q:30}; he "married a French Canadian lady called Monique Bâby", whose portrait still hangs in the family drawing room {q:30, 36}. "I'm going to use the word unstable … he was completely unable to maintain the estate, and he sold it, actually, to his uncle, who was the secretary of one of the Pitts … Sir William Bellingham … And that Bellingham line took over Castle Bellingham" {q:36-38}.

{ctx}Sir William Bellingham (c. 1756–1826) was private secretary to William Pitt the Younger and was made a baronet in 1796 {s:wp-sir-william-bellingham}. Alan married Monique, daughter of the Montreal fur trader Jacques Duperon Bâby, at Detroit in 1795; they separated in 1815; Alan let the estate to his uncle, and after Alan's death in 1821 Monique sold the freehold to Sir William, whose nephews' line then held Castle Bellingham until about 1956 {s:lf-bellingham} {s:wp-bellingham-bt}.

Of Monique the narrator remembered "a very interesting booklet about her life" and a "seaside town" in the West Country whose name escaped him {q:40-42}. {ctx}She settled at Lyme Regis in Dorset after the separation and died there in 1856; the Lyme Regis Museum has published an article on her {s:lf-bellingham}.

"The other boy was Henry … the young army officer. And he was killed at the siege of Badajoz in Spain, in the Peninsular War"; a miniature of him survives "in the other house" {q:44}. Years later his sister Eliza wrote that "her brother Henry was killed on this day, so many years ago" {q:52}. {ctx}Captain Henry Tenison Bellingham was killed in the storming of Badajoz on the night of 6 April 1812 {s:lf-bellingham}, one of the bloodiest assaults of Wellington's Peninsular campaign {s:wp-badajoz}. (The narrator wondered whether it might have been Waterloo {q:48}; that was three years later.)

title: Captain William's household
lede: A soldier-diarist, ten children each born somewhere different, and a slow decline into Dublin lodgings.
body: {p:captain-william-somerville|Captain William Somerville}, born about 1777, married Eliza Bellingham in 1800, when he was 23 {q:60-62}. {ctx}The published genealogy has the wedding at Roscrea on 30 August 1800 {s:lf-bellingham}. He had been "certainly a regular officer as a young man" (family tradition says the South or North Cork Light Infantry, though searches have not confirmed it) and later served in a county militia {q:54-58}.

They had ten children, "eight boys and two girls", "every single one born at a different place, and most of them in [Northern] Ireland" {q:62, 84}. The sons, in so far as their order is known, were {p:william-henry-somerville|William Henry}, {p:archibald-james-somerville|Archibald James}, {p:john-churchill-somerville|John Churchill} (died in infancy), {p:corry-somerville|Corry}, {p:tenison-alan-somerville|Tenison Alan}, {p:bellingham-somerville|Bellingham}, an eighth not named, and {p:samuel-somerville|Samuel}, who died as an infant {q:102-126, 180-182, 190}. Of the two daughters both were called Eliza: the first died in infancy and her name passed to her sister {q:170}.

"Captain William kept a detailed diary … He entered it up every evening, except when he was away from home" {q:132}. In the 1820s the family lived at {pl:cumry|Cumry}, "a small farm" near Ballybay in Co. Monaghan {q:136}; then at a house "just called Farm", apparently near Belturbet in Co. Cavan; then in Dublin, at Bayview Avenue or Crescent on the road to Clontarf {q:182-184}.

The sons were not easy. William Henry, the eldest, "was a ne'er-do-well … fond of the bottle", always in trouble for failing to pay the rent on land he leased from the Brookes in Ulster {q:104-106}. Archibald James and Corry "were fond of women" and fathered several illegitimate children, whose baptisms are marked as such in the registers {q:126-128, 178}. Corry married Lucinda (née Simmonton), who had worked in the Somerville household {q:178-180}.

Eliza died in 1839 {q:186}. "The family then went into decline": the sons were scattered, and only the injured Bellingham remained at home with his father. The two men gave up the Bayview house for lodgings north of the Liffey, where Bellingham died in the autumn of 1844 and Captain William that December {q:196-200}.

title: Flight to the West Indies, and little Archie
lede: A night journey to Dublin, a son gone to sea, a baby with a succession of wet nurses, and a question about a baronetcy.
body: The best-remembered entry in Captain William's diary dates from February 1823. As the narrator recalls it: "Eliza and Dorothea went to Dublin in the car, the night freezing and cold. Eliza and I returned … and we found that when we were away our dear son Archibald had left home, and spent a few days in [Clonmel?], and then took ship on board the George and Thomas for the Barbados" {q:142-150}.

{p:archibald-james-somerville|Archibald James}, then about nineteen {q:18, 112}, "had run away from home because he'd got a girl into the family way. And of course this brought shame on all the family" {q:16-18}. The girl is believed to have been {p:elizabeth-breakey|Elizabeth Breakey}, a servant {q:108-110}.
{int}If the garbled "include Mal" is Clonmel, Archibald may have gone first to his aunt Dorothea, who had married the Clonmel banker William Riall {s:lf-bellingham}, before finding a ship.

"Later in that year 1823 there's mention of a child. A couple of letters were received from Archibald James, one from Madeira, one from Barbados, and one of these letters refers to the child as Archibald. And from then on the child is referred to in the diary as little Archie" {q:154-160}. Remarkably, Captain William and Eliza "assume responsibility for the child, which was unusual, because no responsibility is assumed for any of the other illegitimate children". They paid for "a succession of wet nurses", and the baby was regularly "brought out" to Cumry from Ballybay {q:160-162}.

Was Archibald married? "There is no record of that marriage, but it is constantly referred to by Archibald's sister", Eliza Nelson, in her letters from America {q:168-172}. The narrator's own research led him to believe that Archibald married Elizabeth Breakey, while stressing that "there is no conclusive proof" that little Archie was their son {q:130}.

{int}The narrator then explains why it matters: "The reason that this detail is of great interest is because the Somerville baronetcy became dormant when the then Baron died in January 1929" {q:174}. A dormant baronetcy passes to the nearest legitimate male-line heir who can prove his claim. Archibald was the second son, and the narrator's line descends from the fifth, so legitimate descendants of little Archie, if any exist, would stand ahead of the narrator's line in any such reckoning. The archive records this as the family's reason for interest, not as a claim.
Archibald later moved to Trinidad, where his brothers Tenison and Bellingham followed him; he is said to have died in 1871 {q:128, 194-196}.

title: Tenison Alan: from the sea to the Castle
lede: A cabin boy, a Trinidad sojourn, and a lifetime in the Constabulary secretariat at Dublin Castle.
body: "We are descended from, I think, the fifth son … Tenison Alan, the boy who went to sea" {q:100-102}. He went to sea as a cabin boy and stayed "about five years, from his boyhood until as a young man" {q:14}, then followed Archibald to Trinidad {q:194}. "They were always looking for appointments, particularly in the West Indies" {q:204}.

{int}His first name is transcribed "Tennyson", but it almost certainly honours his grandmother Elizabeth Tenison and his uncle Henry Tenison Bellingham, as "Alan" does his uncle Alan Bellingham {s:lf-bellingham}.

Tenison "returned to Ireland in 1840, after the death of his mother in 1839", and married {p:eliza-oconnor|Eliza O'Connor}, the daughter of a much-married seaman {q:204-208}. He secured a post as an officer "in the Secretariat of the RIC", with "a flat and office in Dublin Castle", the force's headquarters {q:208-210}. The narrator credits "his cousin, Sir William", the Chief Secretary for Ireland, with the appointment {q:212-214}.

{ctx}The force was then the Irish Constabulary, formed in 1836; it became the Royal Irish Constabulary in 1867 {s:wp-ric}. Sir William Meredyth Somerville was Chief Secretary from July 1847 to February 1852 {s:wp-1st-baron}, which suggests that the appointment, if his doing, came several years after Tenison's return (see {qn:q-tenison-appointment}).

"He spent the rest of his life in the RIC." The couple later moved to Rathmines; Tenison died first, and Eliza about 1895 {q:216}. In the narrator's summary he was "a civil servant working in Dublin Castle … well connected, but not wealthy, not landed" {q:330-332}. Two sons are known, both RIC officers: an elder whose name is not recorded, and {p:bellingham-arthur-somerville|Bellingham Arthur} {q:12}.

title: The District Inspector
lede: Riots in the Fenian years, a death at Youghal, a brewer's daughter, and a house at Rathnew.
body: {p:bellingham-arthur-somerville|Bellingham Arthur Somerville} was born in 1856 {q:2}. Like his father and brother he joined the RIC. His early stations were in Cork and Limerick, but most were in Ulster, and he "seemed to have got a name" for attending riots, the "outrages" of his diary, in the 1880s and 1890s, "when the Fenians were at large" {q:290-298}.

{sensitive}The narrator introduced the next story with a caution: "This now is not for publication. Well, I'll let you use your own discretion, but be careful" {q:290}. The events are a matter of public record, and are told here with that request in mind.

In the family's memory: a riot at Youghal "got out of hand", "no doubt over fishing" on the Blackwater; a detachment of RIC went by train from Cork "under the command of Captain Somerville"; and "some rioter called Hanlon or O'Hann" was killed with a blade. Captain Somerville and the constable who struck the blow were held, suspended and relieved of their positions; "the whole thing went as far as Parliament in London"; and he was officially acquitted and reinstated. "It wasn't him that did [it] … it was just his [men], but he was in charge" {q:312-322}.

{ctx}Hansard and local history fill in the rest. On 8 March 1887, during protests at Youghal over the arrest of Fr Daniel Keller, a curate believed to be a trustee of the {t:plan-of-campaign|Plan of Campaign} fund, the RIC charged a crowd with fixed bayonets. {p:patrick-hanlon|Patrick Hanlon}, a 30-year-old fisherman from Ballymacoda, was killed; the cause of death was registered as a "wound inflicted by sword bayonet" {s:ballymacoda-1887}. The coroner's jury returned a verdict of wilful murder against "District Inspector Somerville and Constable Ward", and both men were held in custody in Cork; on 24 March the MP for East Cork asked the Chief Secretary, Arthur Balfour, whether they would be tried at the Cork Assizes, and another member pressed for their suspension from duty {s:hansard-1887}. In the end the Crown entered a nolle prosequi and there was no trial {s:ballymacoda-1887}.

{int}The family's account agrees with the record on almost every structural point: the RIC detachment from Cork (the local District Inspector at Youghal was a Mr Kerin {s:hansard-1887b}), a victim named Hanlon, a blade, arrest, Parliament and no conviction. It differs on the cause (fishing rather than the Plan of Campaign), the weapon (sabre rather than bayonet) and the outcome (an "acquittal" rather than an abandoned prosecution). The published sources name only "District Inspector Somerville"; that he was Bellingham Arthur rests on the family's story, a strong but not documentary identification ({qn:q-youghal-identity}). The death of Patrick Hanlon, a young fisherman, deserves to be remembered in his own right.

With his health failing ("something wrong with his foot or his leg"; gout, or perhaps muscular dystrophy) and a cloud over his career, he asked for a transfer and was posted to Wicklow, where he remained a District Inspector and "never made County Inspector" {q:324-328, 334-336}.

He had married {p:margaret-hall-clinch|Margaret Hall Clinch}, co-heiress with her sister Rachel of Clinch's brewery {q:240, 328-330}. Her father sent barrels of beer to the officers' mess with the name Clinch burnt off, because his daughter was "marrying trade" {q:240}. {ctx}Clinch & Co.'s Eagle Brewery was in Witney, Oxfordshire {s:bhs-clinch}. "She had money, and Bellingham Arthur did not" {q:330}.

Margaret's money made {pl:clermont|Clermont} possible. Bellingham Arthur rented houses around Wicklow until Clermont, at Rathnew, came up for auction. Colonel Tottenham of Ballycurry, who "wanted to have neighbours that he approved of", outbid him, then sold it to him at the price he had paid, "immediately after the auction" {q:572-580}. {ctx}The wings were added in 1894 for "B A Somerville" to designs by Sir Thomas Drew {s:wicklowheritage-clermont}.

He was, in his grandson's words, "very snobbish … very Low Church", and "would have had a fit if he knew that any of his descendants married a Roman Catholic". He kept his children from school altogether {q:338-346}. He died in 1916 of influenza, but not, as the narrator rightly suspected, of the "Spanish flu", which reached Ireland only in 1918 {q:10-12} {s:dcc-flu}.

title: The Clermont generation
lede: Seven children raised without school, five of them soldiers or soldiers' wives, all shaped by the Great War.
body: Bellingham Arthur and Margaret had nine children; two died young {q:228}. The rest were brought up at Clermont: {p:cecilia-somerville|Cecilia} (Aunt Cecil), the eldest; {p:bunt|William Arthur Tenison Bellingham} ("Bunt"), born about 1884; {p:jim|James Aubrey Henry Bellingham} (Jim); a second daughter whose name is unclear, who married {p:edmund-truell|Edmund Truell}; {p:eddie|Adeline} ("Eddie" or "Tete"); {p:pat|Hugh Roger Bellingham} ("Pat"); and the youngest, {p:reginald-somerville|Reginald Malcolm John}, the narrator's father {q:218-228}.

None of them had a normal education: "he never sent any of his children to school". Bunt and Jim went for a short while; Pat and Reginald never went at all {q:344-346}. Cecil became a serious genealogist and in 1912 married her father's solicitor, Henry Rock {q:230-246}. The second daughter married into the Truells of neighbouring Clonmannon, though Edmund chose an English inheritance in Dorset over the Irish estate {q:246-252}. Eddie, "the businesswoman of the family", married late a Royal Engineers officer, "reputed by the family to be the dullest man in the British army" {q:254-260}.

The boys went to the army. Bunt served in India and, after the war, commanded troops at Archangel "to keep it from falling into the hands of the Bolsheviks" {q:362-364}. {ctx}A war-diary-based history records Lt-Col. W. A. T. B. Somerville DSO taking command of the 8th (Special) Battalion, Machine Gun Corps in April 1919; it landed at Archangel on 26 May 1919 {s:mgc-8bn}. Jim was a gunner who spent most of his career in India {q:366}.

Pat was captured "in the retreat from Mons" in August 1914. He escaped three times; the third time "he found his way across Germany, across Holland, and to London", where the War Office took a long time to believe him. He was awarded the Military Cross, but "had a tic for the rest of his life, always looking to see if someone was following" {q:440-450}. He was adventurous and charming, "very unlike his brothers" {q:442-444}.

Reginald was seventeen in 1914 and had "never been outside Clermont really" {q:348-350}. He reached the front in 1916, fought at Passchendaele, "remained a second lieutenant for the entire duration of the war" in the Royal Warwickshire Regiment, and ended up in Italy {q:356-362}. {ctx}The Third Battle of Ypres (Passchendaele) ran from July to November 1917 {s:wp-passchendaele}.

Afterwards, Bunt married Kitty Harrison of Castle Harrison and made a garden near Bantry; Jim married an English wife and lived in Gloucestershire; Pat became a doctor's gardener at Adderbury, near Oxford {q:370-378, 462-464}. "Neither Pat nor my father married money"; Bunt and Jim did {q:494}. All four brothers smoked, and all four died of cancer {q:394, 568-570}.

title: Kenya, loss and a second marriage
lede: An ox cart to Nanyuki, a bride from Laois, a death at sea, and a childhood friend found again.
body: At about twenty-two, with no schooling and no profession, Reginald "decided that he would go to Africa". A company called "Gunners Venture", started by artillery officers after the war, gave him a job managing coffee plantations near {pl:nanyuki|Nanyuki}, "about 120 miles north of Nairobi" {q:496-500}. In 1920 he went up "with an ox cart"; a photograph shows him, "virtually a schoolboy", outside a thatched hut {q:502-504}.

{ctx}"This is a time that East Africa was being opened up to European settlement", as the narrator says {q:498}. Kenya became a Crown colony in 1920, and ex-officers were encouraged to take up land in the highlands around Mount Kenya, land that African communities regarded as theirs {s:wp-kenya-colony} {s:wp-nanyuki}.

Home on leave, he married {p:maud-moore|Maud Moore}, of a County Laois family, in 1928, and took her back to Kenya {q:496, 506-508}. Their daughter {p:juanita|Juanita} was born there in 1932. Two years later, travelling home to show the baby to the family, Maud died on the journey, "so he arrived back in Ireland a widower" {q:508-510}.

Staying at Clermont, he met again "a childhood friend, who was the daughter of the Rector of Wicklow … not having met since they were children, and they got married, and they were my parents": {p:honor-johnson|Honor Johnson} {q:512-514}. The narrator was born in 1937 {q:516}.

title: The end of Clermont
lede: Deaths in quick succession, a tax dispute between two countries, a family quarrel and a sale for £10,000.
body: Under the terms of the will, Clermont was to go to the eldest son, Bunt, if he wanted it; if not, to Jim; and so on down {q:382}. "What actually happened, to cut a long story short, is that everybody died in quick succession": Pat in the 1940s, Margaret in 1949, Jim in 1950 after spending his last year at Clermont, and Bunt about two years after his mother {q:386, 550-552}.

Margaret's estate was complicated: "she was wholly English … she derived all her money from the brewery in England. She lived in Ireland, and there was an argument between the Revenue in Ireland and the Revenue in England as to whether she was domiciled in England or in Ireland" {q:548}. Administration stalled; "nobody seemed to have very much cash" {q:550}. Bunt, the executor, "decided he would like to live there, but he died a matter of months afterwards" {q:554}.

Aunt Eddie wanted Reginald to have the house, but he and Honor "felt they could never afford it". Eddie came close to suing Bunt's widow for his "mess" of the administration; "peace talks" divided the proceeds, half going to the rest of the family {q:558-562}. Clermont sold for "a ridiculous sum now in retrospect, of 10,000 pounds". It had no heating and was badly kept {q:564}. By the time it was finished, "it was about 1950 … '52, '53" {q:566}.

{ctx}Heritage records date the sale to about 1955. In 1956 the Religious of Christian Education opened a convent school there; it closed in the early 2000s, and the site later became a third-level campus linked to Carlow {s:wicklowheritage-clermont} {s:irishaesthete-clermont} {s:wp-rathnew}.

The narrator revisits it with mixed feelings: the beech avenue "like a whole lot of soldiers" is gone; the yard has been "spoilt and pulled down and rebuilt"; the land opposite is covered in houses and an Aldi; and "the fabric of the old house … it's just going", the mortar falling out around the basement {q:530-544}.

title: Kin, namesakes and the road ahead
lede: The Cork Somervilles, the Johnsons, a journalist who is not a cousin, and what remains to be found.
body: Other Somervilles crop up. The interviewer's lecturer knew of "the Somervilles of Cork", who "still live in Drishane House, down in Castletownshend". These are a distinct, "very naval" family, "further off related"; the narrator has met the present owner and his sons {q:280-282, 472-474}. {ctx}Drishane was built around 1780 and is still the family's home; Edith Somerville, the novelist, lived there {s:drishane-southernstar}. The broadcaster Quentin Somerville, the narrator says, is "not in our line, at least" {q:176}.

On the maternal side the narrator's mother Honor was the daughter of the Rector of Wicklow; the interviewer's online tree takes the Johnsons back through a Samuel to a Zachariah (or Samuel the Elder) and a Frances Tench, all needing confirmation {q:518-524}.

The conversation ends with plans: to look through the family's papers together, to visit the Genealogical Office at the National Library, and to finish photographing the portraits that cousin Eliza began {q:46, 272-278, 478}. The open questions collected in this archive are the agenda for that work.
